newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon T-bill investors go longer-term after vote.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon T-bill investors go longer-term after vote.

text.p: Investors in Lebanon are increasingly switching to 24-month treasury bills and the trend to longer-term paper is likely to strengthen in the near future, Beirut bankers said on Monday.
The victory of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri in parliamentary elections has helped boost confidence in the Lebanese currency and prompted more investors to join the shift, they said.
Sales of 24-month t-bills have outstripped shorter-term denominations in the last two weekly issues, rising to 174 billion Lebanese pounds in the latest auction from 117.4 billion the previous week.
The latest auction dated September 5 and announced on Monday totalled 435 billion pounds.
"The shift reflects the market's good perception of the results of the parliamentary elections," Marwan Barakat, head of economic and analysis unit in Bank Audi said.
"The shift is still not very accentuated, but I expect it to continue," he said.
Barakat said increased surpluses of subscription against maturity in recent issues had also boosted trust in the Lebanese market and encouraged more subscription.
The September 5 issue posted a 168 billion pounds nominal surplus compared with 71 billion pounds a week earlier.
Four of the five rounds of the election have been carried out on the past four Sundays amid widespread accusations of fraud but without serious violence. The Bekaa valley votes on Sunday.

"The fact that many of Hariri's supporters have been elected to parliament will make it easier for him to pursue his economic policies which have prevented in the past few years a possible devaluation of the pound," Alain Balian, corporate finance officer at Beirut finance house Lebanon Invest said.
"I expect the trend (into 24-month t-bills) to get stronger after the elections," he added.
"However, with the presence of potential Israeli threats in south Lebanon, the elections cannot be a turning point," Balian said.

The 24-month bills are the longest-term paper offered by Lebanon. They yield 21.74 percent compared with 17.80 percent for 12-month bills, 16.92 percent for six months and 14.61 percent for three months.
